sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
In Wiesbaden, air-quality law and a referendum have shaped traffic policy. An Umweltzone has existed since 2013, and NO2 at the Schiersteiner Straße and Ringkirche stations has roughly halved since 2015 [1]. The city avoided a diesel driving ban when Deutsche Umwelthilfe and the VCD settled their case on 13 February 2019 after the city presented an updated clean-air plan [2]. In a binding referendum on 1 November 2020, 62.1% of voters rejected the Citybahn tram, on a turnout of 46.2% [5]. The mayor said the result must be respected but the traffic status quo cannot remain [5].

Parking regulation is stable. A resident permit costs €120 a year, and visitors can park free for up to an hour in most zones [6]. Deutsche Umwelthilfe considers the fee too cheap and wants at least €360 [7]. In October 2025 the city said it had no plans to extend the parking zone or raise fees, and that the €1.16 million raised from permits in 2024 pays for a discounted pupils' ticket [8]. The new coalition of CDU, FDP, Greens and Volt, agreed in August 2026 with a one-vote majority, plans to review a return to 50 km/h on arterial roads and to test a temporary shutdown of the Berliner Straße traffic-metering light, subject to ratification [29].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The city's own garages have just been rebranded and repriced. From 1 January 2025 WiBau, the municipal parking company, moved its downtown garages to 15- or 20-minute billing steps and cut the Luisenplatz rate from €3 to €2 an hour [9]. It said it would convert all facilities to licence-plate recognition and cashless payment [10]. In December 2025 it introduced 'Lilienparken' as the brand for its facilities, saying the 2025 tariff structure was meant to counter Wiesbaden's image as an 'expensive parking city' [14]. A new Parkhaus Elsässer Platz with 429 spaces has been open since July 2024 [16]. All five Lilienparken garages together have 1,870 spaces, of which 479 have charging points [24]. A 16-point fast-charging park was being built at the Salzbachaue car park near the station, with completion targeted for early September 2026, and we have not confirmed that it opened [23]. For the Advent weekends of 2025 all municipal garages offered a €5 day flat rate [12].

The city counts eleven garages in the centre with 5,106 spaces and five large car parks with 1,490, with guidance boards showing free spaces [20]. Its park-and-ride sites are free, apart from one at Salzbachaue [22]. We found no sourced figures on a shift from the centre to shopping centres.

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
The garages split into three groups: WiBau's Lilienparken, Contipark and Q-Park. Contipark runs the RMCC garage (800 spaces, €2.50 an hour up to €12 a day) [17] and the Kurhaus garage [19]. Q-Park runs the Lili garage with 1,101 spaces beneath the shopping centre by the station [18][21], priced on its own page at €1 an hour in the daytime and up to €10 a day [21], where our price list shows €2.00. Lilienparken's garages in our price list charge a median of €2.00 an hour and €15 a day, and the Kurhaus garage is the dearest garage in our list, at €4.00 an hour. Our data cover 25 garages with 5,324 spaces, eight of them within 500 m of the Schlossplatz (1,921 spaces) and five more within 1 km (1,362).

Occupancy is measured in six garages (2,986 spaces). It averaged 50% on weekdays and 44% at weekends from August to early October 2026. The fullest is the Theater garage (63% on weekdays, 67% at weekends), followed by Markt (56%), RMCC (51%), Coulinstraße (49%), Kurhaus/Casino (46%) and Luisenforum (44%). The three measured garages within 500 m average 56%, against 44% for the three between 500 m and 1 km. Weekend use is far lower at RMCC (33%) and Luisenforum (34%), the two big congress and shopping garages. Capacities in our feed disagree with the city's pages for the Theater garage (158 against 302 to 320) and the RMCC (700 against 800), so their percentages should be read with care. The data cover the summer holidays, so term-time figures may differ, and we have no multi-year history for Wiesbaden.
